questions.question: Test whether a triangle with sides 7, 24 and 25 is right-angled, and say where the right angle is.
questions.expected_answer: The longest side is 25 and 25 squared is 625. The other two give 49 plus 576, which is 625. Equal, so the triangle is right-angled by the converse of the Theorem of Pythagoras, with the right angle between the sides 7 and 24, opposite the 25.

questions.question: Sides 5, 6 and 8: is the triangle right-angled? If not, is it acute- or obtuse-angled?
questions.expected_answer: 8 squared is 64; 5 squared plus 6 squared is 61. Not equal, so not right-angled. Since 64 is greater than 61, the angle opposite the 8 is more than 90 degrees, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.

questions.question: Why must the longest side be the one squared on its own in the test?
questions.expected_answer: The converse compares the square of the side opposite the possible right angle with the other two; the right angle, if it exists, is opposite the longest side. Squaring a shorter side alone compares the wrong quantities and gives a false conclusion, as 5, 12, 13 would wrongly fail.
